new.title: Wander from Rubens to glass art at the Kunstpalast
new.desc: The city's big art museum fills the Ehrenhof, an expressionist brick ensemble built for the GeSoLei exhibition of 1926. Its collection runs from old masters to the Düsseldorf School of painting and on to the Glasmuseum Hentrich, one of the great glass collections.
new.tip: Leave time for the glass rooms, which many visitors skip. Afterwards cross the road to the Rhine meadows behind the Tonhalle.

new.title: Look up at the three slabs of the Dreischeibenhaus
new.desc: Finished in 1960 as the Thyssen headquarters, this 94 metre tower is made of three slim slabs set side by side, and it still counts as one of the finest post-war high-rises in Germany.
new.tip: The best view is from the pond of the Hofgarten at the Landskrone, where the tower reflects in the water.

new.title: Admire the hedge-covered walls of Kö-Bogen II
new.desc: Christoph Ingenhoven's Kö-Bogen II wraps its facades and sloping roof in about eight kilometres of hornbeam hedges, often called the largest green facade in Europe. It faces the white curves of Bernhard Pfau's Schauspielhaus across Gustaf-Gründgens-Platz.
new.tip: Come in autumn, when the hornbeam turns copper, and walk once round the square to see how the old theatre and the new green block talk to each other.

new.title: Visit Jan Wellem's tomb in St. Andreas
new.desc: The former Jesuit and court church on Andreasstraße, cared for by Dominicans since 1972, is a bright baroque space full of white stucco. Behind the choir lies the mausoleum of the Pfalz-Neuburg dukes with the sarcophagus of Elector Johann Wilhelm, the Jan Wellem of the Rathaus statue.
new.tip: Step in on your way between the Altstadt breweries; it is usually quiet even when Bolkerstraße is packed.

new.title: Spot Beuys's stove pipe on the Kunsthalle
new.desc: The Kunsthalle on the Grabbeplatz is a 1967 block of raw concrete that shows changing contemporary art. Look at the wall facing Kay-und-Lore-Lorentz-Platz: a black stove pipe sticks out of it, a work by Joseph Beuys installed in 1981.
new.tip: The Salon des Amateurs bar in the same building is a long-running hangout of art students and DJs, good for a drink after an opening.

new.title: Go underground for art on the Wehrhahn line
new.desc: When the Wehrhahn-Linie opened in 2016, each of its six underground stations was designed by a different artist. At Schadowstraße, Ursula Damm's installation picks up the movements of passengers on LED screens, while Heike Klussmann wrapped Pempelforter Straße in bands of geometry.
new.tip: Buy a short trip ticket and hop between Schadowstraße, Heinrich-Heine-Allee and Graf-Adolf-Platz to compare the stations; outside rush hour you have them almost to yourself.

new.title: Find the painters' graves in the Golzheimer Friedhof
new.desc: Opened in 1805 and closed to new burials in 1884, this old cemetery is now a quiet public park. Under its lime trees lie painters of the Düsseldorf School such as Alfred Rethel and Wilhelm von Schadow, the poet Karl Immermann and Maximilian Friedrich Weyhe, the gardener who laid it out.
new.tip: The grounds are split by Klever Straße; the southern part holds Weyhe's own grave. It makes a calm detour on the way to the Rhine park in Golzheim.

new.title: Browse books in Heinrich Heine's birthplace
new.desc: Heinrich Heine was born at Bolkerstraße 53 on 13 December 1797. Today the house is the Heine Haus, a literature house with readings and the Müller & Böhm bookshop at the front.
new.tip: Check the reading programme on the Heine Haus website, then compare the plaque with the rowdy pub street outside: Heine would probably have enjoyed the irony.

new.title: Step into the old abbey basilica of Gerresheim
new.desc: St. Margareta in Gerresheim was the church of a women's abbey founded back in the ninth century, one of the oldest in the archdiocese of Cologne. The present late Romanesque basilica rises above the old village centre of this former glassmaking town.
new.tip: Walk around the Gerricusplatz and the lanes of old Gerresheim afterwards; the S-Bahn gets you there from the main station in under ten minutes.

new.title: Hear young voices at the Mahn- und Gedenkstätte
new.desc: In the old Stadthaus on Mühlenstraße, the city's Nazi-era memorial centre tells the story of Düsseldorf's children and teenagers under National Socialism through individual life stories.
new.tip: Allow an hour; the personal biographies make it one of the most moving small museums in the Altstadt.

new.title: Warm up under the dome of the Botanical Garden
new.desc: Heinrich Heine University's botanical garden spreads over eight hectares in the south of the city. Its landmark is a glass dome of about 1,000 square metres holding plants from the Mediterranean, the Canary Islands, South Africa, Chile and Australia.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk or bike ride along the Rhine bend at Himmelgeist, one of the most rural corners of the city.

new.title: Drink Schumacher Alt in the Goldener Kessel
new.desc: Brauerei Schumacher's Altstadt outpost on Bolkerstraße brewed its own beer until 1925, and the golden kettle that gave it its name still hangs there. The house was destroyed in 1942 and rebuilt in 1948; today the Alt comes fresh from the mother brewery on Oststraße.
new.tip: It is the calmer, more local choice on Bolkerstraße; ask for a Halve Hahn (a rye roll with Gouda and mustard) with your beer.

new.title: Feast in the courtyard of the Frankenheim brewery tap
new.desc: Heinrich Frankenheim founded his brewery in Pempelfort in 1873, and although brewing on Wielandstraße stopped in 1992, the old Brauereiausschank still pours Frankenheim Alt beside the former brew hall.
new.tip: Come on a warm evening for the big courtyard beer garden, and order the Rinderroulade or the Sauerbraten.

new.title: Line up for ramen at Naniwa
new.desc: In Little Tokyo, the Kobayashi family's Naniwa on Oststraße is one of the city's ramen institutions, with a queue forming outside from lunchtime almost every day.
new.tip: Go mid-afternoon to skip the worst of the queue, and look out for the Japanese grocers and bookshops on nearby Immermannstraße.

new.title: Queue for a scoop at Eiscafé Pia
new.desc: Run by an Italian couple since the early 1970s, Eiscafé Pia on Kasernenstraße in the Carlstadt is the city's classic ice cream parlour, with a long line of house-made flavours.
new.tip: On summer evenings the queue reaches down the pavement; it moves quickly, and the Carlsplatz market and Rhine are both a few minutes away for eating your cone.

new.title: Pick a cake from the window at Café Hüftgold
new.desc: Hüftgold in Flingern turns its shop window into a cake display, from brownie cheesecake to lemon tart, with several vegan and flour-free options. Inside, mismatched teacups and an antler chandelier set the cosy tone.
new.tip: Weekend afternoons are busy; get a slice to take away and stroll the indie shops of Ackerstraße.

new.title: Try the SupaSchoko tart at Kucheneck
new.desc: On Corneliusstraße in Friedrichstadt, Kucheneck is a red and white café in 1970s retro style, known for its rich SupaSchoko chocolate tart and a cheesecake that appears on Sundays.
new.tip: Friedrichstadt is short on tourists, so this is a good stop between the Kö and the Südpark.

new.title: Order a currywurst at Curry in the Medienhafen
new.desc: Curry on Hammer Straße opened in 1999 and calls itself Germany's first currywurst restaurant. It serves the Berlin-style sausage with fries, plus vegan versions, steps from the Gehry buildings.
new.tip: In summer, grab a pavement table and watch the after-work crowd of the Medienhafen go by.

new.title: Treat yourself to gluten-free pastry in Oberkassel
new.desc: Isabella's Pâtisserie on Arnulfstraße bakes only gluten-free, with many cakes that are also vegan or lactose-free, so everyone at the table can share the same tarts.
new.tip: The quark and blackberry tartlet is a bestseller. Afterwards stroll the Art Nouveau streets of Oberkassel down to the Rhine meadows.

new.title: Shop and snack along Ellerstraße in Oberbilk
new.desc: Behind the main station, Oberbilk is the heart of Düsseldorf's Moroccan and Arab community. Ellerstraße, which now carries a second street sign in Arabic, is lined with grocers, bakeries, butchers and grill houses.
new.tip: Pick up fresh flatbread, olives and pastries for a picnic, or sit down for grilled meat and mint tea in one of the side streets.

new.title: Sip a flat white at the Rösterei Vier roastery
new.desc: Rösterei Vier's headquarters on Wallstraße in the Altstadt combine an open roastery, a café, a shop and a co-working space, with beans from different growing regions to compare.
new.tip: Look through to the roaster at work, and buy a bag of house beans as an edible souvenir.

new.title: Taste fresh roasts at Carl Ferdinand in Pempelfort
new.desc: In a former car dealership on Düsselthaler Straße, Carl Ferdinand Röstfabrik puts the coffee bar at the front and the roaster at the back, with single origins and blends explained without any lecturing.
new.tip: Roasting usually happens on Mondays, the best day to catch the smell of fresh beans.
new.q: Carl Ferdinand Röstfabrik Düsselthaler Straße Düsseldorf

new.title: Find the hidden café behind a flower shop in Düsseltal
new.desc: Blumencafé Naskret hides a small café behind a florist's shop, where baker Olga Berger turns out up to 15 kinds of cake a week; her apple cake, Olgas Apfel, is the signature.
new.tip: Sit among the flowers and buy a bunch on the way out; it is a lovely spot for a quiet weekday coffee.

new.title: Learn your beans at Die Kaffee
new.desc: Olga Sabristova has run this private roastery and espresso bar on Schwerinstraße since 2011, with more than 20 coffees, several brewing methods and a rotating cake. Guests may even bring their own food.
new.tip: Ask about the courses on the journey of the bean, and take your time: the shop feels more like a small coffee museum than a café.

new.title: Have waffles on the terrace of the Kaffeeschmiede
new.desc: Near Belsenplatz in Oberkassel, Tamas Fejer's private roastery runs a café with a big terrace that is a neighbourhood favourite, serving its own coffees with waffles, homemade cake and breakfast.
new.tip: Grab a terrace seat on a sunny weekend morning, then walk down Luegallee to the Rhine.

new.title: Hike around the Sengbachtalsperre near Burg
new.desc: Hidden in a side valley of the Wupper close to Schloss Burg, the Sengbach reservoir is one of the oldest drinking water reservoirs in Germany and still supplies Solingen.
new.tip: Swimming is not allowed, but a quiet woodland trail circles the lake; combine it with a coffee in Burg afterwards.

new.title: Hear a concert under the dome of the Tonhalle
new.desc: Düsseldorf's concert hall was built for the GeSoLei exhibition of 1926 as a planetarium, and its great dome now covers the home of the Düsseldorfer Symphoniker.
new.tip: Arrive early to take in the lit dome, and step out to the Rhine promenade at the interval; the riverside setting is part of the charm.

new.title: Laugh along at the Kom(m)ödchen cabaret
new.desc: Founded in 1947 by Kay and Lore Lorentz, the Kom(m)ödchen is one of Germany's best-known political cabaret stages, set in the Kunsthalle building on the square named after its founders.
new.tip: Shows are in German and fast-paced; book well ahead, as the house ensemble's evenings often sell out.

new.title: Watch opera on strings at the Marionetten-Theater
new.desc: In the baroque Palais Wittgenstein on Bilker Straße, the Düsseldorfer Marionetten-Theater plays fairy tales, dramas and even operas with hand-carved puppets for just 90 spectators.
new.tip: The evening shows for adults are the real treat; book ahead, since the tiny hall fills up.

new.title: Catch a variety show under the Rheinkniebrücke
new.desc: Since 1997 Roncalli's Apollo Varieté has staged acrobatics, comedy and live music in a theatre tucked under the Rhine bridge by the state parliament, with a new show every few months.
new.tip: Go for the dinner seats if you want a table; afterwards walk up to the promenade for the lights of the Rheinturm.

new.title: Meet sharks and fossils at the Aquazoo
new.desc: In the Nordpark, the Aquazoo Löbbecke Museum combines a zoo and a natural history museum: around 560 species live in aquariums, terrariums and a tropical hall among fossils and models.
new.tip: It is the city's most visited museum, so arrive at opening on rainy weekends; the Nordpark outside is lovely for a walk afterwards.
new.q: Aquazoo Löbbecke Museum Kaiserswerther Straße Düsseldorf

new.title: Cross the Rhine on the Kaiserswerth ferry
new.desc: North of the city, a small car and bike ferry shuttles across the Rhine between Kaiserswerth and Langst-Kierst in Meerbusch, a slow and scenic alternative to the bridges.
new.tip: Bring a bike: cross over, ride back south along the quiet left bank dykes and return to the centre via the Oberkassel bridge.

new.title: Walk the floodplain of the Urdenbacher Kämpe
new.desc: South of Benrath palace, the Urdenbacher Kämpe is a protected Rhine floodplain of meadows, old river arms, pollarded willows and grazing cattle, one of the wildest landscapes inside the city.
new.tip: Start at Schloss Benrath and walk south; after high water many paths are flooded, so check before you go.

new.title: Watch the fireworks at Japan-Tag
new.desc: Every May or June, Düsseldorf's Japanese community and the city throw a German-Japanese festival on the Rhine promenade that draws over half a million people, with food stalls, martial arts, cosplay and a Japanese fireworks show at night.
new.tip: Stake out a spot on the Oberkassel bank for the fireworks; the view of the rockets over the Altstadt is better and less crowded.

new.title: Place a bet at the Grafenberg racecourse
new.desc: Built from 1909 in the woods of Grafenberg, Düsseldorf's racecourse hosts gallop races on selected Sundays, a tradition going back to the city's first races in 1836.
new.tip: A small bet makes it fun; race days often have family programmes, and the Wildpark is a short walk away.

new.title: Picnic in the Südpark
new.desc: Laid out for the 1987 Federal Garden Show by joining the older Volksgarten with former wasteland, the Südpark is Düsseldorf's largest park at 70 hectares, with themed gardens, playgrounds and wide lawns.
new.tip: Locals bring barbecues and ball games on summer weekends; the farm area is a hit with small children.

new.title: Join the Rundgang at the Kunstakademie
new.desc: Once a year, usually in February, the Kunstakademie on Eiskellerstraße, where Beuys, Richter and Gursky taught or studied, opens every studio to the public for the Rundgang student show.
new.tip: Go on a weekday to avoid the crowds, and keep an eye out: collectors come to spot the next big names.

new.title: See French painting at the Von der Heydt-Museum
new.desc: Founded in 1902 in Elberfeld and named after a family of Wuppertal bankers, the museum is known for nineteenth century French painting and classic modern art, despite the many works seized as 'degenerate' in the Nazi era.
new.tip: Part of the collection rooms are being modernised, so check which floors are open; the Schwebebahn stop Alter Markt is close.

new.title: Explore the Engels family house in Barmen
new.desc: The late baroque Engels-Haus of 1775 belonged to the textile family of Friedrich Engels, who was born about 100 metres away. Reopened in 2021 after a long renovation, it holds a permanent exhibition on his life and work.
new.tip: Combine it with the Museum für Frühindustrialisierung next door, where old textile machines still run.

new.title: Get to grips with tools in Remscheid
new.desc: Remscheid has made tools for centuries, and its Deutsches Werkzeugmuseum in Hasten is the only museum of its kind in Germany, covering hand, machine and power tools from the Stone Age to today.
new.tip: Next door, the baroque Haus Cleff, a 1779 merchant's house, reopened in 2025 after ten years of restoration.

new.title: Circle the moat of Schloss Rheydt
new.desc: Built between 1558 and 1591 by Maximilian Pasqualini, Schloss Rheydt in Mönchengladbach is one of the finest Renaissance moated palaces on the Lower Rhine, and now houses a museum owned by the city.
new.tip: Walk the paths around the moat for the best views, and step into the courtyard to see Pasqualini's Renaissance facades up close.

new.title: Look up at the Quirinus-Münster in Neuss
new.desc: Built between 1209 and 1230, the Quirinus-Münster is the landmark of Neuss, a church in the Rhineland transitional style dedicated to the Roman martyr Quirinus, whose relics arrived in 1050. It was made a minor basilica in 2009.
new.tip: From the Münsterplatz walk on to the Obertor, the city's surviving medieval gate, which houses part of the Clemens Sels Museum.

new.title: Find peace at Kloster Knechtsteden
new.desc: West of Dormagen, this early twelfth century Premonstratensian abbey with its Romanesque basilica of St. Andreas has belonged to the Spiritan missionaries since 1896 and sits among fields and woods.
new.tip: There is a restaurant on the abbey grounds, so it makes a good bike-ride target; the Zons fortress is about eight kilometres away.

new.title: Walk through the Kuhtor into old Kempen
new.desc: The small town of Kempen has kept a compact old centre with the Kuhtor, the last of its four medieval gates, and the castle of the archbishops of Cologne. The Propsteikirche holds the only Renaissance organ front on the Lower Rhine.
new.tip: Have a coffee on the Buttermarkt, then look inside the Propsteikirche for its carved Antwerp altarpieces.

new.title: Discover Burg Brüggen on the Schwalm
new.desc: The brick castle of Brüggen was built to guard a ford over the Schwalm and became the most important castle in the north of the Duchy of Jülich, in a pretty village close to the Dutch border.
new.tip: Combine it with a walk or cycle through the Maas-Schwalm-Nette nature park, full of lakes and heath.

new.title: See the first factory at Cromford in Ratingen
new.desc: In 1783 Johann Gottfried Brügelmann opened a cotton mill in Ratingen named after Arkwright's Cromford, one of the first factories on the European continent. It is now part of the LVR Industrial Museum.
new.tip: Watch the restored spinning machines in action, then visit the merchant's manor house in the park.

new.title: Climb the castle hill of Wassenberg
new.desc: In Kreis Heinsberg, the little town of Wassenberg is crowned by a hilltop castle on its Burgberg, a rare bit of high ground in the flat land near the Dutch border.
new.tip: Walk up from the old town and continue into the woods of the Meinweg area for a longer hike.

new.title: Step back in time at the Dorenburg open-air museum
new.desc: Around the moated Dorenburg in Grefrath, the Niederrheinisches Freilichtmuseum gathers farmhouses and craft buildings from the Lower Rhine on about four hectares, plus a toy museum.
new.tip: Look for the seasonal craft days and markets, when the old houses come to life.

new.title: Climb the Toelleturm above Barmen
new.desc: On the heights of Barmen stands the Toelleturm, an old lookout tower at the top of the Barmer Anlagen, laid out from 1864 by Joseph Clemens Weyhe and the second-largest private park in Germany that is open to everyone.
new.tip: Walk up through the park from the centre of Barmen and come down another way through the Barmer Wald.

new.title: Taste Bolten Alt from a brewery dating itself to 1266
new.desc: In Korschenbroich, the Bolten brewery claims to be the oldest Altbier brewery of all, tracing its brewing rights back to 1266, when the lords of Schloss Myllendonk granted them to a brewer named Heinrich.
new.tip: Order Bolten Alt and Ur-Alt side by side in a local pub, and ride on to the moated Schloss Myllendonk nearby.

new.title: Buy Champagne truffles in Heinemann's home town
new.desc: Konditorei Heinemann was founded in Mönchengladbach in 1932, and its café on Bismarckstraße is a classic stop in town. Its Herrentorte and its Champagne truffles, made since 1968, are its best-known treats.
new.tip: Buy a small box as a gift; the truffles keep for a while, but rarely make it home.

new.title: Bar-hop on Waldhausener Straße in Mönchengladbach
new.desc: Around the Alter Markt and Waldhausener Straße lies Mönchengladbach's old town, the city's main evening quarter, with pubs, bars and clubs packed close together.
new.tip: Start early with a beer on the Alter Markt; regular buses stop late in the evening, so check the night bus.

new.title: Watch the penguins at Wuppertal Zoo
new.desc: Wuppertal's 24 hectare hillside zoo holds around 2,200 animals among old trees in a villa quarter, with apes, big cats, elephants and an underwater tunnel where penguins swim overhead.
new.tip: Take the Schwebebahn to the Zoo/Stadion stop, and wear good shoes: the paths climb steeply.

new.title: See the Tanztheater Wuppertal Pina Bausch
new.desc: Pina Bausch founded her dance company in Wuppertal in 1973 and changed modern dance worldwide. The ensemble still performs her pieces at the Opernhaus in Barmen.
new.tip: Tickets go fast when the season programme is announced; sign up for the newsletter and book early.

new.title: Hear the grindstones at the Balkhauser Kotten
new.desc: One of only two largely original grinding mills left on the Wupper, the Balkhauser Kotten shows how Solingen's blades were ground with water power, and is one of the city's landmarks.
new.tip: Check opening days before going, then walk the Wupper valley path downstream towards the Wipperkotten, the other surviving mill.

new.title: Meet aurochs lookalikes in the Neandertal game park
new.desc: Since 1935, a 23 hectare enclosure in the Neandertal has kept Heck cattle, Heck horses and European bison, animals bred to resemble the aurochs and wild horses hunted by Neanderthals.
new.tip: Entry is free; follow the paths along the fences in the early morning, when the herds are most active.

new.title: Ski in summer at the Neuss indoor slope
new.desc: Opened in 2001, the ski hall in Neuss was Germany's first indoor slope, now run as SnowWorld Neuss and visited by more than a million people a year.
new.tip: Rent gear on site, and book a slot for a hot summer day, when it is the coolest place in the region.

new.title: See Shakespeare at the Globe in Neuss
new.desc: Since 1991 Neuss has held an annual Shakespeare Festival in a replica of London's Globe Theatre on the grounds of its racecourse, with visiting companies from Germany and abroad.
new.tip: The festival usually runs from May into June; bring a cushion and a layer for the evening chill in the wooden galleries.

new.title: Walk around the Hariksee
new.desc: Between Schwalmtal and Niederkrüchten, the Schwalm river flows through this 20 hectare lake, shaped by peat cutting in the seventeenth century and fringed with alder swamps and moors.
new.tip: Walk the shore path, and on another day follow the Schwalm upstream to the Lüttelforster Mühle, an old watermill with an undershot wheel.

new.title: Hike the heath of the Teverener Heide
new.desc: On the Dutch border in Kreis Heinsberg, the Teverener Heide nature reserve is a patchwork of heather, sand, pine woods and small lakes.
new.tip: Come in late summer, when the heather blooms purple; the NATO reconnaissance planes from the nearby Geilenkirchen air base often fly low overhead.

new.title: Ride the steam train of the Selfkantbahn
new.desc: The Selfkantbahn is a metre-gauge museum railway, the last surviving piece of the old Geilenkirchener Kreisbahn, running steam and diesel trains over 5.5 kilometres between Gillrath and Schierwaldenrath since 1973.
new.tip: Trains run on Sundays and holidays from Easter to the end of September; look at the engine sheds in Schierwaldenrath and the buffet car from 1901.

new.title: Feel the Foals' roar at Borussia-Park
new.desc: Borussia Mönchengladbach's stadium in the city's Nordpark holds about 54,000 fans and opened in 2004 in place of the club's old Bökelberg ground.
new.tip: Big home games sell out, so book well ahead; on other days the club offers stadium tours.

new.title: Stroll the gardens of Schloss Dyck
new.desc: Schloss Dyck in Jüchen, ancestral seat of the princes of Salm-Reifferscheid-Dyck, is one of the most important moated castles in the Rhineland, set in an English landscape park over 200 years old with rare trees.
new.tip: Allow a few hours for the park, and come in spring or autumn when the old trees are at their most colourful.

new.title: Watch the stars inside a gas tank in Solingen
new.desc: Near Solingen's main station, a former gas storage tank has become the Galileum, with a planetarium dome, an observatory and a space exhibition including a quarter-scale model of the James Webb telescope.
new.tip: Check the programme for evening shows and observing nights; the children's shows run in the afternoons.

new.title: Walk the crown-shaped park of Schloss Wickrath
new.desc: On the Niers south of Mönchengladbach, baroque Schloss Wickrath was built from 1746 to 1772, and its park is laid out in the shape of a count's crown. The outer wings have stabled horses almost since they were built.
new.tip: Follow the canals around the park and on along the Niers; it is a favourite Sunday walk for Gladbachers.
